newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine chemical, drug firms invest for Mercosur.
newsitem.headline: Argentine chemical, drug firms invest for Mercosur.

text.p: Chemical and drug firms in Argentina plan big investments in the coming year to build up sales to Mercosur, a market which helped them survive a recent Argentine recession, they said in a survey published Tuesday.

In a major business poll by El Cronista newspaper, local units of big players like Dow Chemical, Dupont and Bayer AG stressed their interest in Mercosur, the trade bloc grouping Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay.
All agreed the Argentine recession that ended this year hurt domestic demand. Many, like Germany's BASF, say it demonstrated the wisdom of boosting regional sales.

"We think 1997 will bring new regional opportunities that together with a domestic recovery will allow us to reach our objective for the year of 17 percent higher sales," said BASF Argentina chief Wagner Dieter.

"Our challenge is to take advantage of the positive abroad of the region's future," said David Martin of ICI Argentina, which this year made major acquisitions in Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay from Argentine giant Bunge y Born.

Dow Quimica Argentina, which heads two consortiums that control the newly-privatized Petroquimica Bahia Blanca (PBB) petrochemical complex, plans investments of $450 million in expanding PBB and $500 million on a related pipeline.
The Argentine Dow unit's head Oscar Uberto Vignart said such expansion meant sales for 1996 should soar to $500 million from $90 million last year.

Dow sold its stake in petrochemical firm Indupa this year to Belgium's Solvay. Indupa said it was upgrading its Bahia Blanca facilites to aim for leadership in PVC and sodium chlorate sales in Mercosur.

In the drug industry, Bayer Argentina chief Josef Herbert Nolte told El Cronista that after expected 20 percent higher sales in 1996 versus 1995, Bayer was studying investments of over $50 million "to strengthen our presence" in Mercosur.
Roche Holding AG's local chief Ernest Egli said his profits managed to ride out the Tequila recession "by increasing our sales to the region".
